name: Commitment discounts: reservations and CUDs are where the real GPU price lives, and they are mutually exclusive with spot
region: multi-cloud; savings depend entirely on region and term
price_basis: PERCENT DISCOUNT, not a price - price_usd carries the Azure ND96isr H100 v5 1-year reservation discount of ~36%, derived as stated. Derivation: the Azure Retail Prices API normalised Reservation meter for ND96isr H100 v5 reads $551,221/hour-meter which works out to about $62.88 per instance-hour = about $7.86 per H100-hour against $12.29 on-demand, i.e. ~36% off. AWS Capacity Blocks read $41.528 per instance-hour for p5.48xlarge = $5.191 per H100 (25% off the $6.88 on-demand) and $54.92 for p5en.48xlarge = $6.865 per H200 (13% off). By contrast GCP Spot states credits for Compute Engine do not apply to Spot VMs.
notes: A 13% TO 36% DISCOUNT IS A DIFFERENT PRODUCT, NOT A BETTER PRICE, AND THREE RULES DECIDE WHETHER IT APPLIES TO YOU. (1) COMMITMENT AND SPOT ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE. GCP states plainly that 'credits for Compute Engine don't apply to Spot VMs'. If you modelled a blended rate of spot x (1 - cud), that rate does not exist and your cost estimate is fiction. You choose one instrument or the other. (2) THE HEADLINE DISCOUNT IS NOT THE DISCOUNT YOU GET, AND NOT ALWAYS EVEN OFFERED. Azure's own VM pricing page shows '-' in BOTH the 1-year and 3-year savings-plan columns for ND96isr H100 v5, while the Retail Prices API's normalised reservation meter implies ~36% off. That is a real conflict between two first-party Azure surfaces and the honest reading is that the derived figure is indicative of the reservation meter's mechanics, not an offer. Read the reservation meter, not the marketing page, and treat a reservation that does not appear on the pricing page as something to confirm with sales. (3) TERM AND UTILISATION DECIDE, AND THE COMMITMENT IS A LIABILITY. A 1-year reservation for a GPU you stop using is a year of paying for an idle H100. The repo's own energy record is the reminder: an idle 8xH200 node still draws 41.7% of its loaded watts, so an under-utilised reservation burns money twice - once in the reservation and once in the power bill for GPUs that are paid for and not busy. Use reservations for a baseline of continuously-needed capacity and spot for the burst above it; do not reserve the burst. AWS Capacity Blocks sit between the two instruments and are the right tool when the pool must still be there tomorrow without a year-long commitment - the p5 allocation problem is precisely why they exist.
